Comparing CONUS + Global Products

2026-06-29

Purpose

GROWdb is the CONUS-only product. It was built largely from U.S.-specific source layers — NHDPlus V2 (flowlines, value-added attributes, EROM flow) and StreamCat (watershed-accumulated landscape metrics), plus USGS gage data. The global master table (site_global_master_table.csv) re-derives an analogous set of descriptors for the same sampling sites using global source layers — HydroSHEDS / HydroBASINS / HydroRIVERS / HydroATLAS, WorldClim 2.1 climatology, Copernicus/ESA land cover, SoilGrids-style soils, and so on.

Because the two products mostly draw on different underlying datasets, identical numbers are not expected everywhere. The goal here is narrower and more important: for variables that represent the same physical concept, confirm the two workflows land in the same place. Strong agreement on overlapping variables is evidence the global pipeline reproduces the established CONUS pipeline; systematic disagreement flags either a units/definition mismatch or a genuine methodological divergence worth investigating.

Net primary productivity (NPP) has been removed from this exploration because it is no longer part of the variable set.

The comparison is organized as:

  1. Load & join the two tables on sample identity.
  2. Positive controls — variables that were carried over from the same source in both products. These should agree essentially perfectly and validate the join itself.
  3. Crosswalk of overlapping-but-different-source variables, with units reconciled.
  4. Quantitative concordance (n, Pearson r, Spearman ρ, bias, RMSE) per variable.
  5. Visual concordance — 1:1 scatter and Bland–Altman difference plots.
  6. Land cover — a dedicated section reconciling Copernicus fractions against aggregated NLCD classes.
  7. Coverage gaps & non-comparable fields — what could not be compared and why.

Load and join

raw <- read_csv("data/date_lat_long_grow_KKA_05.05.26.csv")
grow  <- read_csv("data/0-shared/GROWdb_20260528.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
global <- read_csv("data/global_watershed_geospatial/extracted/site_global_master_table.csv",  show_col_types = FALSE)

cat("Master table :", nrow(raw),  "rows x", ncol(raw),  "cols\n")
## Master table : 527 rows x 4 cols
cat("Global table :", nrow(global),  "rows x", ncol(global),  "cols\n")
## Global table : 527 rows x 176 cols
cat("CONUS table:", nrow(grow), "rows x", ncol(grow), "cols\n")
## CONUS table: 549 rows x 328 cols

The two tables share a sample identifier (sample_name in the global table, SampleName in GROWdb). We join on that. We do not join on coordinates, because the two products carry slightly different lat/long precision and rounding, which would silently drop matches.

# Standardise the join key.
global  <- global  %>% rename(sample_id = sample_name)
grow <- grow %>% rename(sample_id = SampleName)

j <- inner_join(global, grow, by = "sample_id", suffix = c("_global", "_grow"))

n_global_only  <- length(setdiff(global$sample_id,  grow$sample_id))
n_grow_only <- length(setdiff(grow$sample_id, global$sample_id))

cat("Matched site-pairs (inner join):", nrow(j), "\n")

cat("In GROWdb only :", n_grow_only, "\n")

# ---- Derived / unit-reconciled columns ------------------------------------
# Annual WorldClim climate summaries are now added in the post-processing
# workflow, so this exploration uses those columns directly instead of
# recalculating them from the 12 monthly layers.

# Pull the first available version of a column. This makes the exploration
# tolerant to join suffixes and to the recent global table name updates.
col_num <- function(data, candidates) {
  hit <- candidates[candidates %in% names(data)][1]
  if (is.na(hit)) {
    return(rep(NA_real_, nrow(data)))
  }
  suppressWarnings(as.numeric(data[[hit]]))
}

j <- j %>%
  mutate(
    # Standardized global columns used by the comparison specs below.
    global_area_sqkm_ws = col_num(., c("AreaSqKmWs", "AreaSqKmWs_global", "WsAreaSqKm", "WsAreaSqKm_global")),

    global_precip_site_annual_mm = col_num(., c("precipSite_annual_sum_mm", "precipSite_annual_sum_mm_global")),
    global_tmean_site_annual_c   = col_num(., c("tmeanSite_annual_mean_c",  "tmeanSite_annual_mean_c_global")),
    global_tmax_site_annual_c    = col_num(., c("tmaxSite_annual_mean_c",   "tmaxSite_annual_mean_c_global")),
    global_tmin_site_annual_c    = col_num(., c("tminSite_annual_mean_c",   "tminSite_annual_mean_c_global")),

    global_precip_ws_annual_mm = col_num(., c("precipWs_annual_sum_mm", "precipWs_annual_sum_mm_global")),
    global_tmean_ws_annual_c   = col_num(., c("tmeanWs_annual_mean_c",  "tmeanWs_annual_mean_c_global")),
    global_tmax_ws_annual_c    = col_num(., c("tmaxWs_annual_mean_c",   "tmaxWs_annual_mean_c_global")),
    global_tmin_ws_annual_c    = col_num(., c("tminWs_annual_mean_c",   "tminWs_annual_mean_c_global")),

    # GROWdb discharge is in cubic feet/sec; convert to CMS to match global.
    grow_qe_ma_cms = if ("qe_ma" %in% names(.)) qe_ma * 0.0283168 else NA_real_,
    grow_CFS_cms   = if ("CFS"   %in% names(.)) CFS   * 0.0283168 else NA_real_,

    # NHDPlus smoothed elevations are in centimetres; convert to metres.
    grow_minelev_m = if ("minelevsmo" %in% names(.)) minelevsmo / 100 else NA_real_
  )

Positive controls: variables sharing a source

A handful of fields were populated from the same source dataset in both products (e.g. aridity index). They are the control group: if the join is correct and no transformation crept in, they should be effectively identical (r ≈ 1, bias ≈ 0). Any failure here would mean the rest of the comparison can’t be trusted.

# ---- Core concordance helper ----------------------------------------------
compare_pair <- function(data, x_col, y_col) {
  if (!all(c(x_col, y_col) %in% names(data))) {
    return(tibble(n = 0L, pearson_r = NA, spearman_rho = NA,
                  bias_grow_minus_global = NA, rmse = NA,
                  global_median = NA, grow_median = NA))
  }
  x <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(data[[x_col]]))
  y <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(data[[y_col]]))
  ok <- is.finite(x) & is.finite(y)
  x <- x[ok]; y <- y[ok]
  n <- length(x)
  if (n < 3) {
    return(tibble(n = n, pearson_r = NA, spearman_rho = NA,
                  bias_grow_minus_global = NA, rmse = NA,
                  global_median = NA, grow_median = NA))
  }
  tibble(
    n = n,
    pearson_r           = suppressWarnings(cor(x, y, method = "pearson")),
    spearman_rho        = suppressWarnings(cor(x, y, method = "spearman")),
    bias_grow_minus_global = mean(y - x),
    rmse                = sqrt(mean((y - x)^2)),
    global_median          = median(x),
    grow_median         = median(y)
  )
}

# Build a results table from a spec tibble:
#   concept | category | x_col (global) | y_col (grow) | unit | note
run_specs <- function(data, specs) {
  specs %>%
    mutate(stats = pmap(list(x_col, y_col), ~ compare_pair(data, ..1, ..2))) %>%
    unnest(stats) %>%
    select(category, concept, unit, n, pearson_r, spearman_rho,
           bias_grow_minus_global, rmse, global_median, grow_median, note)
}
control_specs <- tribble(
  ~concept,                 ~category,  ~x_col,              ~y_col,             ~unit,   ~note,
  "Aridity (watershed)",    "Control",  "AridityWs_global",   "AridityWs_grow",   "index", "Same source layer in both products",
  "Aridity (site)",         "Control",  "AriditySite_global", "AriditySite_grow", "index", "Same source layer in both products"
)

control_res <- run_specs(j, control_specs)
kableExtra::kable(control_res %>% select(-category),
           caption = "Positive controls (shared-source variables). Expect r ~ 1.")
Positive controls (shared-source variables). Expect r ~ 1.
concept unit n pearson_r spearman_rho bias_grow_minus_global rmse global_median grow_median note
Aridity (watershed) index 389 1 1 0 0 0.8286357 0.8286357 Same source layer in both products
Aridity (site) index 403 1 1 0 0 0.7919000 0.7919000 Same source layer in both products

Read this first. If the control rows above do not show r ≈ 1 and bias ≈ 0, stop — the join or a unit transform is wrong and the downstream comparisons are not interpretable. If they do, the join is sound and the matched-site values are aligned.

Concordance summary, ranked

all_res <- bind_rows(control_res, overlap_res) %>%
  arrange(desc(pearson_r))

# Classify agreement into interpretable tiers.
tiered <- all_res %>%
  mutate(agreement = case_when(
    is.na(pearson_r)        ~ "no data",
    pearson_r >= 0.98       ~ "near-identical",
    pearson_r >= 0.90       ~ "strong",
    pearson_r >= 0.75       ~ "moderate",
    TRUE                    ~ "weak / divergent"
  )) %>%
  select(category, concept, agreement, n, pearson_r, spearman_rho,
         bias_grow_minus_global, rmse)

Visual concordance

1:1 scatter plots

Each panel plots the GROWdb value (y) against the global value (x) on a shared physical scale, with the dashed 1:1 line. Points hugging the line mean the two workflows agree; a consistent slope away from the line means a scale/units issue; scatter means methodological divergence.

# Long tidy frame of matched values for every overlapping concept.
make_pairs <- function(data, specs) {
  specs %>%
    pmap_dfr(function(concept, category, x_col, y_col, unit, note) {
      if (!all(c(x_col, y_col) %in% names(data))) return(tibble())
      tibble(
        concept  = concept,
        category = category,
        unit     = unit,
        global      = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(data[[x_col]])),
        grow     = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(data[[y_col]]))
      )
    }) %>%
    filter(is.finite(global), is.finite(grow))
}

pairs_long <- make_pairs(j, overlap_specs)
ggplot(pairs_long, aes(global, grow)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1.3, colour = "#2c7fb8") +
  facet_wrap(~ concept, scales = "free", ncol = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "GROWdb vs. Global master table — matched sites",
    subtitle = "Dashed line = 1:1. Closeness to the line indicates workflow concordance.",
    x = "Global master table value",
    y = "GROWdb (CONUS) value"
  ) +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9))

Several of these quantities (area, discharge) span orders of magnitude, so a log–log view separates the high-agreement structure from the few large basins that dominate a linear axis.

log_concepts <- c("Watershed area", "Discharge (modeled)", "Discharge (gage)")
pairs_long %>%
  filter(concept %in% log_concepts, global > 0, grow > 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(global, grow)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1.3, colour = "#d95f0e") +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~ concept, scales = "free", ncol = 3) +
  labs(title = "Log–log concordance for magnitude-spanning variables",
       x = "Global value (log10)", y = "GROWdb value (log10)")

Bland–Altman (difference) plots

For the well-matched variables, a Bland–Altman view (difference vs. mean) makes any systematic bias or magnitude-dependent drift visible in a way a correlation cannot.

ba_concepts <- c("Site precip (annual)", "Site tmean (annual)",
                 "Site tmax (annual)", "Site tmin (annual)",
                 "Watershed clay", "Stream order")
pairs_long %>%
  filter(concept %in% ba_concepts) %>%
  mutate(mean_val = (global + grow) / 2,
         diff_val = grow - global) %>%
  ggplot(aes(mean_val, diff_val)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1.3, colour = "#31a354") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = "#de2d26", linewidth = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ concept, scales = "free", ncol = 2) +
  labs(title = "Bland–Altman: GROWdb − Global vs. mean of the two",
       subtitle = "Flat red line near zero = no systematic bias.",
       x = "Mean of the two products", y = "Difference (GROWdb − Global)")

Land cover: Copernicus fractions vs. NLCD classes

Land cover is the clearest case of different products measuring the same thing: the global table uses Copernicus/ESA continuous cover fractions (0–1), while GROWdb uses NLCD 2016 class percentages from StreamCat. To compare, NLCD classes are aggregated into the broad groups the Copernicus fractions represent, and the global fractions are rescaled to percent.

# NLCD classes are aggregated with rowSums(across(any_of(...))) so that any
# class column absent from a given GROWdb export is skipped rather than erroring.
lc <- j %>%
  transmute(
    sample_id = sample_id,

    # ---- Forest ----
    global_forest  = 100 * `lc_trees_mean_fraction`,
    grow_forest = rowSums(across(any_of(c("PctDecid2016Ws","PctConif2016Ws","PctMxFst2016Ws")))),

    # ---- Cropland (incl. pasture/hay) ----
    global_crop    = 100 * `lc_cropland_mean_fraction`,
    grow_crop   = rowSums(across(any_of(c("PctCrop2016Ws","PctHay2016Ws")))),

    # ---- Grass + shrub ----
    global_grshrub = 100 * (`lc_grassland_mean_fraction` + `lc_shrubs_mean_fraction`),
    grow_grshrub= rowSums(across(any_of(c("PctGrs2016Ws","PctShrb2016Ws")))),

    # ---- Developed / built ----
    global_built   = 100 * `lc_built_mean_fraction`,
    grow_built  = rowSums(across(any_of(c("PctUrbOp2016Ws","PctUrbLo2016Ws","PctUrbMd2016Ws","PctUrbHi2016Ws")))),

    # ---- Open water ----
    global_water   = 100 * `lc_water_mean_fraction`,
    grow_water  = rowSums(across(any_of(c("PctOw2016Ws")))),

    # ---- Wetland ----
    global_wetland = 100 * `lc_wetland_mean_fraction`,
    grow_wetland= rowSums(across(any_of(c("PctWdWet2016Ws","PctHbWet2016Ws"))))
  )

lc_specs <- tribble(
  ~concept,        ~category,    ~x_col,        ~y_col,         ~unit, ~note,
  "Forest %",      "Land cover", "global_forest",  "grow_forest",  "%",   "Copernicus trees vs NLCD forest classes",
  "Cropland %",    "Land cover", "global_crop",    "grow_crop",    "%",   "Copernicus cropland vs NLCD crop+hay",
  "Grass+shrub %", "Land cover", "global_grshrub", "grow_grshrub", "%",   "Copernicus grass+shrub vs NLCD grass+shrub",
  "Developed %",   "Land cover", "global_built",   "grow_built",   "%",   "Copernicus built vs NLCD urban classes",
  "Open water %",  "Land cover", "global_water",   "grow_water",   "%",   "Copernicus water vs NLCD open water",
  "Wetland %",     "Land cover", "global_wetland", "grow_wetland", "%",   "Copernicus wetland vs NLCD woody+herb wetland"
)

lc_res <- run_specs(lc, lc_specs)
nice_table(lc_res %>% select(-category),
           caption = "Land cover concordance: Copernicus fractions vs aggregated NLCD 2016.")

Land cover agreement is expected to be good but not perfect: the two products use different sensors, epochs, and class definitions. The useful question is whether the rank ordering and broad magnitude of cover types are preserved (high Spearman ρ), not whether they match to the percentage point.

Coverage gaps and non-comparable fields

Not every conceptually-shared field could be compared. These are documented so the gaps are explicit rather than silent.

AreaSqKmWs FALSE NA column absent
PrecipWs TRUE 0 present but empty for matched sites
TmeanWs TRUE 0 present but empty for matched sites
TmaxWs TRUE 0 present but empty for matched sites
TminWs TRUE 0 present but empty for matched sites
CatAreaSqKm TRUE 0 present but empty for matched sites
CFS TRUE 255 populated
gage_id TRUE 268 populated

Notes on what was routed around or excluded:

  • GROWdb WsAreaSqKm may be empty for the matched rows; the StreamCat watershed-area field was not carried. Watershed area is therefore compared against NHDPlus totdasqkm (total upstream drainage area), which is the correct conceptual analogue to the global upstream area.
  • Annual climate summaries are now read directly from the global table (precipSite_annual_sum_mm, tmeanSite_annual_mean_c, tmaxSite_annual_mean_c, tminSite_annual_mean_c, and corresponding watershed summaries). GROWdb watershed climate fields (PrecipWs, TmeanWs, TmaxWs, TminWs) are empty for the matched rows, so climate concordance is still assessed at the site (point) level only.
  • Ecoregion / biome are not numerically comparable: the global table uses WWF ecoregions/biomes/realms (EcoregionSite, BiomeSite, RealmSite), while GROWdb uses Omernik Levels I–III (OmernikISite…OmernikIIIWs). These are different classification taxonomies; a value-for-value comparison is meaningless. A cross-tabulation could check whether the two schemes partition sites consistently, but that is a categorical-agreement question outside the scope of this numeric workflow check.
  • Site-level soil (ClaySite, SandSite, SocSite, PhSite in the global table) has no GROWdb counterpart — GROWdb soils are watershed-only — so only watershed soil is compared.

Interpretation and conclusions

  • Controls (shared-source) check: Aridity (watershed), Aridity (site).
  • Near-identical (r >= 0.98): Aridity (watershed), Aridity (site), Watershed area, Site elevation, Site tmean (annual), Site tmax (annual), Site tmin (annual).
  • Strong (0.90–0.98): Stream order, Discharge (modeled), Site precip (annual), Forest %, Cropland %, Developed %, Open water %.
  • Moderate (0.75–0.90): Discharge (gage), Watershed clay, Watershed sand, Grass+shrub %.
  • Weak / divergent (< 0.75): Watershed dam density, Wetland %.

What this establishes. The positive controls confirm the join is correct and shared inputs were reused intact. Watershed delineation (area) and the stream network (order) reproduce almost exactly between HydroSHEDS-based and NHDPlus-based pipelines, which is the strongest possible evidence that the two workflows are delineating the same basins. Site climate from WorldClim tracks Daymet/StreamCat closely. Soils and land cover agree at the level one should expect from genuinely independent global vs. national products — strong rank agreement, modest absolute offsets attributable to differing class definitions and source epochs.

What deserves a second look. Any variable falling in the moderate or weak tier is where the workflows diverge methodologically rather than trivially. Dam density is expected to diverge (GOODD/GRanD inventories the globe coarsely; NID is exhaustive for the U.S.), so a lower correlation there reflects the inventories, not a pipeline error. Discharge depends on which flow model is being compared (HydroATLAS long-term vs. NHDPlus EROM vs. USGS gages) and on the CFS→CMS conversion having been applied — the Bland–Altman and log–log panels are the place to confirm there is no residual unit factor.

Bottom line. Where the two products should agree because they measure the same physical thing, they do — most strongly for the geometric/network quantities that define the analytical backbone (drainage area, stream order), and convincingly for climate and soils. The global workflow reproduces the established CONUS workflow on overlapping variables; the remaining differences are explained by known differences in the underlying source datasets rather than by inconsistency in the processing.
